title: Servants, Stewards, and Fools for Christ
summary: Paul tells the Corinthians to regard apostles as servants of Christ and stewards of God's mysteries, whose only judge is the Lord. He exposes their pride with sharp irony: they act as if they already reign, while the apostles are treated as the scum of the earth. He then speaks as their father in the faith, urges them to imitate him, announces that he is sending Timothy, and warns that he will come soon to test the arrogant, asking whether he should come with a rod or with love.
story: This chapter closes the first major section of the letter (1:10-4:21), on divisions in the church. Chapter 3 described leaders as servants and fellow workers, and warned that God will test every builder's work. Chapter 4 draws out the consequences. If leaders are stewards answerable to God, the Corinthians have no business ranking them, and Paul will not accept their judgment of him. The chapter moves from argument to appeal, as Paul turns from teacher to father. It also sets up the rest of the letter: Paul's announced visit gives weight to the corrections he will make in chapters 5 and 6.
historical:
Paul was writing from Ephesus around AD 53 to 55. He had sent Timothy, his younger coworker, ahead through Macedonia (Acts 19:22), and in 16:10 he speaks of Timothy possibly arriving after the letter. Timothy had helped found the Corinthian church (Acts 18:5; 2 Corinthians 1:19). Paul's plan to come soon, "if the Lord is willing", was fulfilled only in part and with difficulty; 2 Corinthians describes a painful visit and changed travel plans.

The hardships Paul lists in verses 11 to 13 match what Acts and his other letters report. He worked with his own hands as a tentmaker (Acts 18:3; 20:34), went hungry and thirsty, was beaten, and had no settled home. By the time he wrote this letter he had been imprisoned at Philippi and driven out of several cities. He describes these not as bad luck but as the normal shape of apostolic life.
cultural:
Several of Paul's images come from Roman social life. A steward (oikonomos) was usually a trusted slave or freedman who managed a household's affairs on behalf of the master. What mattered most in a steward was faithfulness, since he handled what belonged to someone else. The guardian (paidagogos) in verse 15 was a slave who escorted a child to school and supervised his conduct, a familiar but not always respected figure. A father, by contrast, had lasting authority and a unique bond. Paul claims that role because he brought them to faith.

The picture in verse 9 draws on the spectacles of the Roman world. In a triumphal procession for a victorious general, captives were led at the rear, and some were executed at its end; in the arena, condemned criminals were often brought out last to die. Either way, Paul pictures the apostles as condemned men on display before the world, angels, and people. The words translated "scum" and "refuse" in verse 13 referred to what is scraped off or swept away, and some writers used them for people considered worthless. Manual labor, which Paul chose, was looked down upon by many educated people, who expected a teacher to be supported by patrons or fees.
literary: The chapter moves in four steps. Verses 1 to 5 define apostles as servants and stewards and reject premature judgment. Verses 6 and 7 state the purpose of the preceding chapters and ask three probing questions, the sharpest being "What do you have that you did not receive?" Verses 8 to 13 are heavy with irony: "Already you have all you want. Already you have become rich." Paul contrasts the Corinthians' imagined status (wise, strong, honored) with the apostles' real condition (foolish, weak, dishonored), then lists apostolic hardships and responses in a rhythmic series (vilified, we bless; persecuted, we endure; slandered, we answer gently). Verses 14 to 21 shift to a tender and firm parental appeal, ending with a question that leaves the choice to the Corinthians.

outline.t: Stewards judged by the Lord, not by people
What do you have that you did not receive?
A father's appeal and the sending of Timothy
A warning to the arrogant: rod or love

doctrines.note: The Lord is the only judge of his servants. He will come, bring hidden things to light, and reveal the motives of hearts, and then each will receive praise from God. Until then, believers should not pass final judgment on one another.

Church leaders are servants of Christ and stewards of God's mysteries, accountable for faithfulness. Their authority is real, as Paul's fatherly warning shows, but it is exercised in love and patterned on the humility of Christ.

The apostles' hunger, homelessness, and mistreatment are not signs of failure but of faithfulness to a crucified Lord. Paul sets their suffering against the Corinthians' belief that they had already arrived.

words.note: Oikonomos, steward or household manager. It combines oikos, house, and nomos, law or management, and is the source of the English word economy. A steward managed his master's property and was judged by his faithfulness. Paul applies it to apostles as stewards of the mysteries of God.

Huperetes, servant or assistant, originally perhaps a rower on a ship and later any subordinate who carried out the orders of another. Luke uses it for the servants of the word (Luke 1:2). Paul uses it with oikonomos to stress that apostles are under Christ's orders.

Peripsema, what is wiped off, scum or refuse. The word could also refer to a person regarded as worthless, and in some Greek usage to a victim offered to cleanse a community. Paul uses it to describe how the world sees the apostles, a deliberate contrast with the Corinthians' sense of their own importance.

Mimetes, imitator, from which English gets mimic. Paul urges the Corinthians to imitate him, as he says in 11:1, because he imitates Christ. In a culture where students imitated their teachers, this was a call to follow a way of life, not only a set of ideas.

christ: The chapter shows Christ as the Lord who judges and whose pattern shapes his servants. Apostles are servants "of Christ" and stewards of God's mysteries, and the Lord who comes will expose what is hidden and give each person his praise (verse 5). The apostles' life of hunger, homelessness, blessing when reviled, and enduring persecution mirrors the life of Jesus, who had nowhere to lay his head and blessed those who cursed him. Paul says “in Christ Jesus I became your father through the gospel” (verse 15), so his fatherhood is derived from Christ and exercised on his behalf. The kingdom of God consists not in talk but in power (verse 20), the power Paul has already identified in 1:18 and 1:24 with the message of the cross and with Christ himself.

hard.q: Isn't it arrogant for Paul to tell people to imitate him?
hard.a:
To modern ears, "I urge you to imitate me" can sound self-important. In the ancient world, however, teachers routinely offered themselves as models, and students learned by watching how their teachers lived. Paul's call is shaped by the rest of the chapter. The life he asks them to imitate is not one of success and honor but of weakness, hard work, humility, and blessing in the face of abuse. He describes himself as a fool, weak, dishonored, and the refuse of the world. In 11:1 he makes the source of his example explicit: he asks them to imitate him as he imitates Christ.

Paul also refuses to judge even himself (verses 3 and 4). His conscience is clear, but that does not justify him; only the Lord's judgment counts. So his call to imitation does not rest on a claim to perfection but on his being a father who embodies the gospel he preached. The request is a test for any leader: a leader can only rightly say it if what people see in them is the shape of the cross.

questions: Paul asks, "What do you have that you did not receive?" How would taking that question seriously change the way you think about your gifts and achievements?
Paul says he does not even judge himself. What would it mean to live without either inflating or condemning yourself, leaving final judgment to the Lord?
Who has been a father or mother in the faith to you, and in what ways has their life, not only their words, shaped yours?
